# Shared changed-file fixtures: git's three NUL-separated listings turned
# into the review pane's (status, path, old_path) triples.
#
# The SAME rules live twice right now — internal/host/review.go and
# app/src/diffsource.zig — and this file is what stops them drifting.
# Both test suites read it and must agree on every row.
#
# These parsers are worth pinning this hard for two reasons. They are
# INDEX-WALKING loops over a flat field array, where rename records
# consume a variable number of fields — the classic place to lose a file
# or spin. And the status vocabulary is not the same in both formats,
# which is the sort of asymmetry a second implementation quietly
# "corrects" (see the C rows below).
#
# When the port completes and one implementation is deleted, this file
# stays: it is the spec for the parse, not scaffolding for the migration.
#
# Format, '|'-separated, fields trimmed:
#
#   name | parser | input | want
#
# parser: which listing the input came from.
#   porcelain  — `git status --porcelain -z`      (head mode)
#   namestatus — `git diff --name-status -z REF`  (branch mode)
#   others     — `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z`
#
# input: the listing's raw bytes, with two escapes so the fields can be
#   trimmed and read by eye — `\0` is NUL and `\s` is a space. Both
#   matter: NUL is the separator, and a leading space is a MEANINGFUL
#   porcelain status ("\sM" is modified-unstaged, "M\s" is staged).
#
# want: comma-separated `status:path` in order, or `status:path<-oldpath`
#   for a record that carries a rename/copy origin. The literal EMPTY
#   means "no files" — spelled out, so a blank field is a typo rather
#   than an assertion.
#
# Both parsers assert they read exactly this many cases, so a row one
# side skips is a failure rather than a silent gap.
# cases: 32

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- porcelain
#
# One record per path: the XY pair carries the staged state in X and the
# worktree state in Y, and a single path is listed once however many of
# the two moved. The pair is folded to ONE word, and the worktree side
# wins a mixed verdict — what is on disk now is what you are about to
# review.

porcelain modify unstaged             | porcelain | \sM\sf.txt\0                | modified:f.txt
porcelain modify staged               | porcelain | M\s\sf.txt\0                | modified:f.txt
porcelain modify both sides           | porcelain | MM\sf.txt\0                 | modified:f.txt
porcelain add staged                  | porcelain | A\s\snew.txt\0              | added:new.txt
porcelain add intent-to-add           | porcelain | \sA\sf.txt\0                | added:f.txt
porcelain delete unstaged             | porcelain | \sD\sgone.txt\0             | deleted:gone.txt
porcelain delete staged               | porcelain | D\s\sgone.txt\0             | deleted:gone.txt
porcelain typechange                  | porcelain | \sT\sf.txt\0                | modified:f.txt
porcelain unmerged                    | porcelain | UU\sf.txt\0                 | modified:f.txt
porcelain untracked                   | porcelain | ??\su.txt\0                 | untracked:u.txt

# Added, then deleted from disk before anyone looked: the worktree side
# wins, so this reads deleted. Ordering inside the fold is the whole
# content of this row — a fold that tested A before D would say added,
# and the pane would offer to diff a file that is not there.
porcelain worktree side wins          | porcelain | AD\sboth.txt\0              | deleted:both.txt

# Renames and copies put the ORIGIN in its own following field, so the
# walk consumes two fields for one file.
porcelain rename                      | porcelain | R\s\snew.txt\0old.txt\0     | renamed:new.txt<-old.txt
porcelain rename then edited          | porcelain | RM\snew.txt\0old.txt\0      | renamed:new.txt<-old.txt

# A COPY carries an origin exactly like a rename, and is still reported
# `modified` — because the fold only spells R as renamed. Deliberate: a
# copy did not move the original, so the pane has a new file whose
# interesting diff is against the file it was copied from. Note this is
# the OPPOSITE of what name-status does with C, two sections down.
porcelain copy keeps its origin       | porcelain | C\s\scopy.txt\0src.txt\0    | modified:copy.txt<-src.txt

# Paths are NOT quoted or escaped in -z mode, so a space in a name is
# just a byte in the path — the record ends at the NUL and nowhere else.
porcelain path containing a space     | porcelain | \sM\sdir/a\sb.txt\0         | modified:dir/a\sb.txt
porcelain two files                   | porcelain | \sM\sa.txt\0\sM\sb.txt\0    | modified:a.txt,modified:b.txt

# A record too short to hold "XY path" is skipped rather than sliced —
# and the walk carries on to the next one instead of giving up on the
# rest of the listing.
porcelain runt record is skipped      | porcelain | \sM\0\sM\sb.txt\0           | modified:b.txt
porcelain clean tree                  | porcelain | EMPTY                       | EMPTY

# --------------------------------------------------------------- namestatus
#
# `git diff --name-status -z` puts the status in its OWN field, so a
# plain record is two fields and a rename/copy is three. Same file list,
# an entirely different field rhythm from porcelain.

namestatus modify                     | namestatus | M\0f.txt\0                 | modified:f.txt
namestatus add                        | namestatus | A\0new.txt\0               | added:new.txt
namestatus delete                     | namestatus | D\0gone.txt\0              | deleted:gone.txt
namestatus typechange                 | namestatus | T\0f.txt\0                 | modified:f.txt

# The status field carries a similarity score, so the letter is a PREFIX
# and never the whole field.
namestatus rename with score          | namestatus | R100\0old.txt\0new.txt\0   | renamed:new.txt<-old.txt

# ...and here C reads `renamed`, where porcelain reads `modified`. Both
# sides must reproduce the inconsistency until someone decides which is
# right; a port that unified them would change what the pane says about
# copies without anyone choosing that.
namestatus copy reads renamed         | namestatus | C085\0src.txt\0copy.txt\0  | renamed:copy.txt<-src.txt

namestatus two records                | namestatus | M\0a.txt\0A\0b.txt\0       | modified:a.txt,added:b.txt

# The rhythm change mid-listing is the thing: three fields, then two.
# An advance that assumed one width would read the next status as a path.
namestatus rename then modify         | namestatus | R100\0o.txt\0n.txt\0M\0f.txt\0 | renamed:n.txt<-o.txt,modified:f.txt

namestatus no changes                 | namestatus | EMPTY                      | EMPTY

# Truncated tails. Neither can come from a healthy git, and neither may
# loop or read past the end. A status with no path yields NOTHING — an
# empty path is not a file, and a blank row in the pane that reports a
# diff nobody can open is worse than a dropped record.
namestatus status with no path        | namestatus | M\0                        | EMPTY
namestatus rename missing its target  | namestatus | R100\0o.txt                | modified:o.txt

# ------------------------------------------------------------------- others
#
# Untracked files, folded into branch mode: work that is part of the task
# even though nobody has run `git add` yet.

others two files                      | others | a.txt\0b.txt\0                 | untracked:a.txt,untracked:b.txt
others nothing untracked              | others | EMPTY                          | EMPTY
others empty fields are not paths     | others | a.txt\0\0b.txt\0               | untracked:a.txt,untracked:b.txt
